v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.name: La Voile - La Reserve Ramatuelle
v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.why: La Réserve Ramatuelle is the clifftop hotel of Michel Reybier — the industrialist behind Cos d'Estournel — and Canino's cooking descends from Michel Guérard, who invented 'cuisine minceur' in the 1970s to make fine dining light; that spa-hotel provenance is why the plates read as clarity, not richness.
v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.verdict: This is the most decorated kitchen on the Saint-Tropez peninsula and it earns the fireworks by subtraction rather than excess, cooking in the wellness lineage that shaped it. Falsifiable claim: La Voile holds two MICHELIN stars in the 2026 MICHELIN Guide France.
v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.signature: Whatever garden-and-day-boat course is running, the crudites and vegetable plates, then a line-caught fish; Canino built his name on making a tomato or a courgette taste like the whole coastline.
v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.caveat: Price and booking: hotel-restaurant, menu-led prices well into three figures; dinner reservations essential and summer books solid. It closes out of season, so a winter visit finds it dark.
v-la-voile-la-reserve-ramatuelle.hook: The peninsula's high altar of clear, olive-oil cooking, in a room that seems to float between the umbrella pines and the sea.

signal_chip.label: MICHELIN TWO STARS
signal_chip.full: Two MICHELIN Stars, MICHELIN Guide France 2026
signal_chip.cosign: Chef Eric Canino, in the Michel Guerard 'cuisine minceur' lineage

v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.name: La Palmeraie — Château de Valmer
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.why: Château de Valmer is no invented backdrop: it is a 19th-century wine estate producing its own AOC Côtes de Provence rosé, where the dining room sits inside a botanical park of listed palms and the restaurant runs only when the summer estate opens its doors.
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.address: Château de Valmer, 81 boulevard de Gigaro, 83420 La Croix-Valmer, France
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.verdict: A one-star Relais & Châteaux dining room under a grove of century-old palms above Gigaro, where Alexandre Fabris builds three Provençal set menus — one entirely vegetarian — around vegetables, herbs and flowers just-picked from the estate's organic potager. Confirmed one star in the 2026 Michelin Guide France, and open only for the summer season.
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.signature: "Les meilleurs légumes de notre potager" — the estate's just-picked vegetables read three ways on one plate: cooked but still crisp, in purée, and raw. The garden, not a protein, is the headline.
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.caveat: Not a casual drop-in, and not in Cavalaire itself — it sits above Gigaro in La Croix-Valmer, opens only 8 May–4 October (2026), serves set menus at destination prices, and fills fast. Book well ahead; there is no walk-in stretch of the season.
v-la-palmeraie-chateau-de-valmer.person: Alexandre Fabris — Burgundy-born, raised in his family's restaurant La Billebaude in Givry; trained under Lameloise, Meneau and Marcon; at Château de Valmer since 2021, having earned his first star in 2019 at La Signoria in Calvi.

signal_chip.label: 1 Michelin star · Guide France 2026
signal_chip.full: One Michelin star in the 2026 Michelin Guide France; also selected among the Saint-Tropez peninsula's gourmet tables by Yonder (2025).

v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.name: Vista — Lily of the Valley
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.why: Vista is the gastronomic table of Lily of the Valley, the Philippe Starck-designed wellness resort that opened on the Gigaro hillside in 2019 — a hotel built around fitness and longevity, which is why even its fine-dining leans light and sun-first rather than rich.
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.address: Lily of the Valley, Colline Saint-Michel, Bd Abel Faivre, Quartier de Gigaro (Plage de Gigaro), 83420 La Croix-Valmer, France
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.verdict: Order the Sisteron lamb shoulder braised with savory (€98, to share) and you'll taste why Gault&Millau gives it 13/20 (2026); à la carte runs roughly €25–150 a plate at a five-star hotel table with a sea-facing terrace — not a Michelin star it doesn't hold.
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.signature: Sisteron lamb shoulder braised with savory (sarriette), served to share (€98) — the dish both Gault&Millau and the Michelin selection single out.
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.caveat: This is a 5-star hotel dining room, not a hidden bistro: à la carte runs roughly €25–150 a plate and the room holds about 120 covers between the hall and its sea-facing terrace, so the draw is Maillard's cooking and the view, not intimacy. No Michelin star — it's in the Michelin selection only (the hotel itself holds two Michelin "clés"). The earlier "John Dory with chickpeas" isn't confirmed on current menus — chickpea fries, broccoli guacamole and a fisherman's catch are — and I could verify a sweeping Mediterranean sea view but not a literal 180° sweep over the Îles d'Or; treat that view claim as unverified.
v-vista-lily-of-the-valley.person: Vincent Maillard — head chef at Lily of the Valley since the hotel opened in 2019, trained under Guy Savoy and Alain Ducasse (Louis XV, with Franck Cerutti) and ex-Byblos Saint-Tropez; Gault&Millau "Techniques d'Excellence PACA 2022."

signal_chip.label: Gault&Millau 13/20
signal_chip.full: Gault&Millau 13/20 (2026 review): 'a festive place for insiders, away from the crowds of Ramatuelle or Saint-Tropez.'
signal_chip.cosign: Warm review on Gilles Pudlowski's site (2022: 'assiettes gorgées de soleil… paradis provisoire'); hotel also featured in Yonder's curated 'most beautiful hotels with views on the Côte d'Azur' (Pauline Duvieu).

v-les-saisonniers.name: Les Saisonniers
v-les-saisonniers.why: It is the couple's first place of their own — Florent Manini and Anna Thillaye left the security of a Saint-Tropez palace kitchen to gamble on a small village room, which is why the carte stays short and personal rather than palace-formal.
v-les-saisonniers.address: Boulevard de Tahiti (Les Palmiers II), 83420 La Croix-Valmer — in the village, above the municipal pool
v-les-saisonniers.verdict: Three-star-trained pastry precision at village-bistro prices (~€45-60 a head), on a short, market-driven carte that turns with the season. Order the pumpkin tartlet under goat-cheese ice cream or the ratatouille-stuffed squid. Wrong choice only if you need a sea view or a table open all week.
v-les-saisonniers.signature: Fine pumpkin tartlet with goat-cheese ice cream (and the squid stuffed with ratatouille) — the pastry-trained hand shows in both.
v-les-saisonniers.caveat: The carte is short and rotates with the season, so the pumpkin tartlet or the ratatouille squid may not be on the day you go. It's a village room above the municipal pool, not a seafront table; the draw is the cooking, not a horizon. Opening days are limited — roughly Wed-Sat, lunch and dinner, plus a weekend brunch — and sources split on whether it opened February or March 2024.

signal_chip.label: Gault&Millau + Michelin Guide, 2025
signal_chip.full: Listed in the Michelin Guide France 2025 with a Plate ('good cooking') — a selection, not a star or Bib — and recommended by Gault&Millau. Opened early 2024 (sources split February/March). Both chefs trained under Arnaud Donckele at the 3-star La Vague d'Or (Cheval Blanc Saint-Tropez); Florent was pastry chef there ~7 years and did winters at Sebastien Vauxion's 2-star Sarkara in Courchevel.

v-les-saisonniers._lane: Out of the palace kitchens — two chefs' rooms

v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc.name: Le Parc — L'Hôtel du Parc
v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc.why: The old Hôtel du Parc was gutted and reborn as a Tuscan-style villa-hotel, and this bistronomic table under the pines came with the reinvention — the town's first credible sit-down grew out of a hotel makeover, not a chef arriving cold.
v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc.verdict: In a town with no Michelin table, this is the one credible sit-down. Chef Jean-Brice Ruffroy, a veteran of starred kitchens, runs a bistronomic carte off named Provençal produce — Provence asparagus, Sisteron lamb, Perthuis potatoes — and the pêche du jour, served in the dining room or on the terrace over the park. Falsifiable: if you sit down and the menu isn't built on that named local sourcing plus a daily catch, this card is wrong.
v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc.signature: Label Rouge pork with artichokes and phô broth — the dish Gault&Millau flags first as the signature; the pêche du jour (daily catch) carries the fish billing.
v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc.caveat: The signal is a selection and a phrase, not a rating: Gault&Millau lists it with no toque and no /20 score published, and there is no Michelin nod — a resort town this size barely registers with the guides (Michelin: zero starred tables in Cavalaire). Naming is muddled too (the room reads as 'Le Parc'; the dinner service is branded 'La Table du Parc'). And note the honest mismatch: the guide-flagged marquee dishes are actually meat and fruit (Label Rouge pork, coquelet, apricot three ways) despite the fish-forward billing. It's a 4-star hotel restaurant — evening-focused, not a cheap eat — and seasonal: the dining room runs roughly late April to early October (closed Mondays), while in winter the chef and brigade decamp to Avoriaz.

signal_chip.label: Gault&Millau: the region's 'place to be'
signal_chip.full: Gault&Millau calls the reborn Hôtel du Parc the region's 'place to be' and chef Jean-Brice Ruffroy 'a poet of southern flavors' — a G&M selection, but with no toque or /20 score published (fr.gaultmillau.com, 2025).
signal_chip.cosign: Jean-Brice Ruffroy, chef (schooled in gastronomic and starred kitchens)

v-le-parc-l-hotel-du-parc._lane: Out of the palace kitchens — two chefs' rooms

v-la-pinede-plage.name: La Pinède Plage
v-la-pinede-plage.why: Feet near the sand, the Îles d'Or on the horizon, octopus under lemon confit.
v-la-pinede-plage.address: 382 Boulevard de Gigaro, 83420 La Croix-Valmer, France
v-la-pinede-plage.verdict: The most credible feet-near-the-sand table on Gigaro. A pine-shaded terrace facing the Îles d'Or where the octopus arrives cooked in court-bouillon, dressed as a carpaccio under a lemon-confit condiment with capers, tomato, rocket and pine nuts, alongside a tuna niçoise and shellfish linguine. Be clear about what it is: not a gastronomic temple. Gault&Millau gives it one toque and 12/20 — the mark of a very good beach kitchen, not a great restaurant. But on a shore where most tables coast on the view alone, this one actually cooks, and cooks with produce from the Château de Valmer's own kitchen garden.
v-la-pinede-plage.signature: Octopus cooked in court-bouillon, served carpaccio-style with a lemon-confit condiment, capers, tomato, rocket and pine nuts (the dish Gault&Millau leads its review with); the house "burger de la Pinède" is the casual counterpoint on the same card.
v-la-pinede-plage.caveat: This is the restaurant of a 4-star hotel's private beach: resort pricing, a yacht-stopover crowd (Gault&Millau notes it accommodates "yachtsmen on stopover"), and a short season — it runs only 30 April to 10 October (2026 dates confirmed), shut the rest of the year. One honest note on the signal: Gault&Millau's live page dates the 12/20 / one-toque rating to 2025, not 2026, so it is the current guide's score but carries a 2025 stamp. The executive menu is Thomas Pézéril's; the hotel's own site names Massimiliano d'Amico as the chef executing it day to day.

signal_chip.label: Gault&Millau 12/20
signal_chip.full: Gault&Millau: 12/20, 1 toque, listed as a Gourmet Restaurant (rating dated 2025 on the live gaultmillau.com page, verified)

v-la-pinede-plage._lane: On the sand — Gigaro and the Grande Plage

v-marius-a-la-plage.name: Marius à la plage
tags: Beach restaurant, pieds dans l'eau (contemporary Provençal + grilled fish)
productTags: Beach restaurant, pieds dans l'eau (contemporary Provençal + grilled fish)
v-marius-a-la-plage.why: Arthur and Sarah ran an earlier 'Le Marius' at the port for two years before moving in 2012 to this Gigaro beach — the very sand where the couple's own story began, so the homecoming is theirs as much as the grandfather's.
v-marius-a-la-plage.address: Plage de Gigaro, 83420 La Croix-Valmer (Golfe de Saint-Tropez, near Cavalaire-sur-Mer)
v-marius-a-la-plage.subcat: Beach restaurant, pieds dans l'eau (contemporary Provençal + grilled fish)
v-marius-a-la-plage.verdict: The tables sit literally on the sand in the preserved bay at the far end of Gigaro, feet from the turquoise. Contemporary Provençal cooking built on freshly caught, grilled Mediterranean fish; in high summer, live musical apéritifs often run around 7–9pm. Run by Arthur and Sarah since April 2012.
v-marius-a-la-plage.signature: Calamars grillés — grilled squid with sauce vierge and homemade ratatouille (EUR 28); the sardines grillées de Méditerranée with ratatouille (EUR 24) run the same grilled-fish line. The house dessert "Douceur du Père Marius" (EUR 12) nods directly to the grandfather the place is named for.
v-marius-a-la-plage.caveat: No Michelin or Gault&Millau listing, and no curated-journalism review surfaced in verification — this earns its place on genuine local reputation, not a guide badge. And you pay for the sand-and-sea setting: a tartare de bar main runs about EUR 49, grilled fish around EUR 24–28. Seasonal — open roughly early April (around 6 April) to the end of September; music times shift by night, so call ahead (04 94 54 25 05).
v-marius-a-la-plage.person: Arthur and Sarah — founders since April 2012, after two years running "Le Marius" at the port; named for Arthur's grandfather Marius, and set on the Gigaro beach where the couple's own story began.
v-marius-a-la-plage._lane: On the sand — Gigaro and the Grande Plage

v-tamaris-beach.name: Tamaris Beach
v-tamaris-beach.why: The tonnelle de paille is the roof and the lapping water is the soundtrack — you order the fish because it was landed nearby, not because the kitchen is reaching for anything.
v-tamaris-beach.address: Promenade de la Mer, 83240 Cavalaire-sur-Mer, France
v-tamaris-beach.verdict: Come for a feet-in-the-sand lunch under the straw tonnelle on Cavalaire's main beach: a salad or a plancha-grilled local fish, water lapping a few metres away, open daily in season from 9h (closing between 18h and 20h depending on the source). It's an honest beach table, not a kitchen with ambition — arrive expecting gastronomy and you'll be let down; the fish and the sand are the whole point.
v-tamaris-beach.signature: Poisson local grille a la plancha — locally caught fish on the plancha, the anchor of a short card of salads and grilled meats and fish.
v-tamaris-beach.caveat: No Michelin or Gault&Millau listing, and none should be expected — this is a plage-privee lunch spot, not a gastronomic address. Seasonal only (published dates 30 March to 5 November); a day package of two loungers and a parasol runs about EUR 42 and a midday meal about EUR 25, so it's a beach-club sit-down, not cheap eats. No owner or chef is named in any source.

signal_chip.label: Little Weekends · city guide
signal_chip.full: Named in the curated Cavalaire-sur-Mer 'bonnes adresses' guide by French travel site Little Weekends, which sets the scene precisely: tables under a straw tonnelle right on the sand a few metres from the sea, a card of fresh salads, grilled meats and locally caught fish on the plancha, open daily in season 9h-18h (beach directories list closing as late as 20h). A curated travel guide, not a rating body — no year is bylined on the page, and it reads as a minor editorial listing rather than a Michelin- or Fooding-calibre review.
